					STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPERIOR COURT Merrimack, ss MBC Ventures, LLC. Clerk's Notice of Decision Document Sent to Parties on 12/08/2020 v. WIRELESS LINK,INC.; and JAWED SHAIKH 217-2019-CV-00613 FINAL ORDER The matter before the court is defendants’ Revised Motion To Dismiss. Defendants argue that (a) New Hampshire law provides the applicable statute of limitations, (b) that statute is the three-year statute for personal actions, RSA 508:4, and not, as plaintiff maintain, the twenty-year statute for and contracts under seal, RSA 508:5, and (c) this action was filed after the three year limitation period. For the reasons set forth below, the court agrees with defendant that RSA 508:4 is the applicable statute of limitations and that it expired before this action was filed. PREJUDICE. According, the complaint is DISMISSED WITH I. FACTS ALLEGED IN THE COMPLAINT A. The 2013 Line Of Credit Agreement And Personal Guaranty This is a suit for breach of a loan agreement and an associated personal guaranty agreement. In September 2013, defendant Wireless Link, Inc. (“Wireless”) obtained a $100,000 line of credit, good for one year, from Bank of America. Wireless signed a contract captioned “Line of Credit Agreement”(“the 2013 Agreement,” Complaint Ex. A). Wireless’ president, defendant Jawed Shaikh, signed the 2013 Agreement in his personal capacity as a guarantor. Section 8.2 of the 2013 Agreement provides that, except to the extent federal law may apply, the agreement shall be governed and interpreted under North Carolina law. The incorporated guaranty agreement (i.e. Section 9 of the 2013 agreement) contains similar language providing that “this personal guaranty is governed by federal law and the laws of North Carolina.” 2 Shaikh’s personal guaranty agreement also states that “This Personal Guaranty is intended to take effect as an instrument under seal.” It was signed by defendant Shaikh as guarantor with the word “seal” in parenthesis after his name. Shaikh signed a second time, on behalf of Wireless, and once again his signature was followed by the word “seal” in parenthesis. However, the document does not have a wax seal, a wafer seal, an embossed seal, a stick-on seal, or any other indicia of sealing. B. The 2014 Amended And Restated Loan Agreement In October 2014, Wireless and Bank of America entered into an Amended and Restated Loan Agreement (“the 2014 Agreement,” Complaint Ex. B). The 2014 Agreement did not extend the line of credit. Indeed, it expressly stated that “The revolving line of credit feature is closed and will not be re-opened. All amounts outstanding, once repaid, may not be reborrowed.” However, the deadline for repayment of principal and interest was extended by until October 3 13, 2015. In all other respects pertinent to this case, the 2014 Agreement replaced the 2013 Agreement with regard to Wireless’ obligations. See 2104 Agreement, Preface B. The 2014 Agreement left Shaikh’s personal guaranty in place. That guaranty, as originally drafted and signed expressly applies to “any modifications or replacements” of the underlying line of credit agreement). Further, the 2014 Agreement contains a Consent, signed by Shaikh in his individual capacity as guarantor. Section 7.2 of the October 2014 agreement contains a choice of law provision that makes New Hampshire (not North Carolina law) controlling. The 2014 Agreement does not purport to be made under seal. It was signed by Shaikh in his capacity as President of Wireless. after his name. The word “seal” does not appear The Consent, signed by Shaikh in his individual capacity, does not purport to be signed under seal. There is no other indicia of a seal. 4 C. Breach Wireless defaulted on its payment obligations. Bank of America’s rights under the 2013 and 2014 Agreements were assigned several times, most recently to the plaintiff. The plaintiff filed this action on September 13, 2019, more than three years from the date of Wireless’ breach. II. LEGAL ANALYSIS A. New Hampshire Law Provides The Statute Of Limitations For Plaintiff’s Claim Against Wireless Plaintiff’s claim against Wireless must be brought under the 2014 Agreement rather than the 2013 Agreement. That is so because the 2014 Agreement replaced the 2013 Agreement with respect to (a) Wireless’ repayment obligations and (b) dispute resolution. The 2014 Agreement contains a choice of law provision stating that New Hampshire law controls. This court must honor that provision. See Hobin v. Coldwell Banker Residential Affiliates, 144 N.H. 626, 628 (2000) (“Where parties to a contract select the law 5 of a particular jurisdiction to govern their affairs, that choice will be honored if the contract bears any significant relationship to that jurisdiction.”); see also In Re Scott, 160 N.H. 354, 364 (2010); Coldwell Banker Real Estate, LLC v. Brian Moses Realty, Inc., 752 F. Supp.2d 148, 164 (D.N.H. 2010). In this case, the 2014 agreement bore a clear relationship to New Hampshire because Shaikh lived in this state and seemingly operated Wireless in this state. The fact that the earlier 2013 Agreement was governed by North Carolina law is beside the point. B. New Hampshire Law Also Provides The Statute Of Limitations For Plaintiff’s Claim Against Shaikh Wireless’ breach of guaranty claim against Shaikh is brought under the guaranty agreement incorporated within the 2013 Agreement (i.e. Section 9 of the 2013 Agreement). As noted above, the guaranty agreement survived intact even after the 2014 Agreement otherwise replaced the 2013 Agreement. The guaranty agreement 6 included its own choice of law provision that requires the court to apply North Carolina law. However, while North Carolina law applies to the substance of the claim against Shaikh (i.e. to the elements that plaintiff must prove to establish liability, to the measure of damages, and to the elements of defenses and affirmative defenses), this court must apply New Hampshire procedural law. Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc., 131 N.H. 6, 12 (1988); Bartlett v. Commerce Insurance Company, 167 N.H. 521, 526(2015). The New Hampshire Supreme Court generally treats statutes of limitations as procedural for choice of law purposes. See Waterfield v. Meredith Corporation, 161 N.H. 707, 710 (2011) (“[W]e generally treat statutes of limitations as procedural statutes and accordingly apply our own law.”); Gordon v. Gordon, 118 N.H. 356, 360 (1978) (“We have long followed the general rule that a statute of limitations is a matter of procedure and as such the law of the forum applies.”). 7 To be sure, a limitations period can sometimes be an intrinsic, inseparable and vital part of another state’s statutory scheme for the determination of liability. In such cases, the limitations period may be substantive, see Keeton, 131 N.H. at 13-14, but this is not such a case. In this case the plaintiff asserts a generic North Carolina common law claim (i.e. breach of contract) that is subject a generic limitations period. It is also true that New Hampshire courts will engage in a multi-factored choice of law analysis regarding a limitations period in the odd case in which both (a) no party is a New Hampshire resident and (b) the cause of action did not arise in New Hampshire. Keeton, 131 N.H. at 15. However: [I]n any case in which either party is a New Hampshire resident or the cause of action arose in this State, the sum of our above stated forum interests in applying our own statute, in combination with the benefit of simplification afforded by regular application of our own rule, will tip the choice of law balance in favor of the application of our own limitations period to cases tried here. Thus, in such cases, our courts may typically apply the 8 relevant New Hampshire statute without appeal to our choice-influencing considerations. Id. In this case, the defendants are both New Hampshire residents. Therefore, pursuant to the Keeton line of cases, New Hampshire law provides the applicable limitations period for plaintiff’s claims against Shaikh. C. The Applicable Statute Of Limitations Is RSA 508:4 (“personal actions”), Not RSA 508:5 (“specialties”) Wireless and Shaikh claim that the applicable statute of limitations is RSA 508:4. That statute provides a three year limitations period for personal actions, “except as otherwise provided by law.” The breach of contract claims in this case are archetypical personal actions. See State v. Lake Winnipesaukee Resort, LLC, 159 N.H. 42, 48(2009) (noting that while the term “personal action” is not defined by statute it includes common law contract claims). Plaintiff argues that a different limitations period is “otherwise provided by law.” More 9 particularly, plaintiff points to RSA 508:5 which provides a twenty year limitations period for “actions of debt upon judgments, recognizances, and contracts under seal.” Thus, the court must determine whether either the 2014 Agreement (at issue in plaintiff’s claim against Wireless) or the 2013 guaranty agreement (at issue in plaintiff’s claim against Shaikh) is a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. This is an easy question to answer with respect to the 2014 Agreement. The 2014 Agreement does not bear an actual or embossed seal and it contains no language or graphics suggestive of a seal. Therefore, the 2014 Agreement is a plain vanilla contract and the claim for its breach is subject to three year limitations period in RSA 508:4 for personal actions. The analysis of the 2013 guaranty agreement is more complicated. As noted above, although the document does not bear a physical seal, or even an embossed seal, the fine print states that “This Personal Guaranty is intended to take effect as an instrument 10 under seal.” Additionally, the preprinted form includes the word “seal” in parenthesis following the line for Shaikh’s signature. While the relevant New Hampshire case law is sparse, and the controlling precedent dates from another era, it is nonetheless clear that these expedients are insufficient to create a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. The case most on point is Burns Mortgage Company v. Hardy, 94 F.2d 477, 480–81 (1st Cir. 1938). In Burns, the assignee of a note brought suit for its breach. The defendant was the borrower who resided in New Hampshire at the time of the suit. The note was executed in a different state (Florida), where it qualified as a contract under seal. However, the only indicia of a seal was the word “seal” in parenthesis after the borrower’s signature. Both parties in Burns agreed, and the First Circuit held, that the action was governed by the applicable 11 New Hampshire statute of limitations.1 They disagreed, however, about whether that statute was New Hampshire’s (then) six-year statute for “personal actions” or New Hampshire’s twenty-year statute for “contracts under seal.”2 Thus, the question presented in Burns was the same one that confronts the court today. In Burns the First Circuit held that what constitutes a “contract under seal” within the meaning 1 See Burns, 94 F.2d at 480–81: [T]o the extent the validity of a seal affects the obligation of a contract it is to be tested by the lex loci contractus; but to the extent that it affects the remedy for the enforcement of the contract in a forum other than the one in which it was made, including the statute of limitations of such forum, it is to be tested by the law of the forum— the lex fori. 2 In 1938, when Burns was decided, the two statutes of limitations were codified as P.L. 329:3 and 4. P.L. 329:3, which provided the limitations period for personal actions was later recodified without change as RSA 508:4. Subsequent to recodification, the Legislature shorted the limitations period from six to three years. P.L. 329:4 provided the limitations period for suits on contracts under seal. It was later recodified without change as RSA 508:5 and has never been amended. 12 of the New Hampshire statute of limitations is a question of New Hampshire law: It cannot, with reason, be contended that the Legislature of New Hampshire, in enacting section 4 [of P.L. 329, presently codified as RSA 508:5], intended that the words “contracts under seal” should define or embrace any contracts other than those which were regarded by the laws of New Hampshire to be contracts under seal. It surely did not mean to include within those words contracts which might be regarded as under seal by the laws of Florida, statutory or otherwise, or of any other state or country. Burns, Id., at 480. In support of this holding, Burns cited, inter alia, New Hampshire Supreme Court precedent from 1833. In Douglas v. Oldham, 6 N.H. 150, 150 (1833) our Supreme Court held that regardless of where a contract was executed, New Hampshire law will determine whether, for procedural purposes, it was made under seal. Although the New Hampshire Supreme Court has not revisited this issue in close to 200 years, Douglas (and by extension Burns) appears to represent a consensus view among American courts. See, Restatement (Second) Conflict of Laws, §142, comment a (“So if the forum statutes prescribe different periods of 13 limitation for . . . actions on sealed and unsealed instruments, the local law of the forum will be applied to determine whether . . . an instrument is under seal.”); 16 Am. Jur. 2d Conflict of Laws § 95 (“[W]here the question is whether the instrument sued on is a sealed instrument and an action thereon accordingly not barred by limitations, the sufficiency of the seal is to be so tested [by the law of forum]”); Eric Mills Holmes, Stature and Status of A Promise Under Seal As A Legal Formality, 29 Willamette L. Rev. 617, 633 (1993): The law of the forum (and not the law of the state of execution) determines matters of remedy and procedure. If that law regards an instrument bearing the word “seal” in parentheses as not “under seal,” the statute of limitations applicable to unsealed contracts applies. This is true even if the state of execution regards the contract as “under seal” and therefore allows a longer period of limitations. See also President and Directors of Georgetown College v. Madden, 505 F. Supp. 557, 581 (D. Md. 1980) (“[T]he forum's law would be applied to determine, in a limitations context, if the contract was sealed, though the law of the place of contracting would be 14 applied if the question of whether the document was sealed involved a substantive right such as ‘the sufficiency of the instrument as title.’”); Wallbaum v. Martin, 234 A.2d 369 (R.I., 1967)(a promissory note executed in Pennsylvania, that contained the words “witness our hand and seal” and the word “seal” in parenthesis next to the signatures, was not a contract under seal within the meaning of the Rhode Island statute of limitations even though it qualified as such in Pennsylvania); Gaffe v. Williams, 22 S.E.2d 512, 513 (Ga, 1942); Leonor v. Ingenio Porvenir C. por A., 34 N.Y.S.2d 705, 709 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1942); Alropa Corp. v. Kirchwehm, 33 N.E.2d 655, 657 (Ohio, 1941); Coral Gables v. Christopher, 189 A. 147, 149 (Vermont, 1937); Alropa Corp. v. Rossee, 86 F.2d 118, 119 (5th Cir. 1936). Thus, the only remaining question in this case is whether the guaranty agreement is a contract under seal within the meaning of New Hampshire law. It is not. As explained below, New Hampshire requires either a 15 physical or embossed seal and the guaranty agreement contains neither. In Burns, the First Circuit recited the District Court’s determination, which was not appealed by either party, that under New Hampshire law a “contract under seal” must bear a physical wax seal or a physical wafer: [U]nder the law of New Hampshire, the law of the forum, an instrument not bearing a wax seal or wafer is not a specialty or contract under seal. Burns, 94 F.2d at 478. The only pertinent New Hampshire authority cited for this proposition by the First Circuit and the District Court was Douglas v. Oldham. In Douglas (which to refresh the reader’s recollection was decided in 1833), the New Hampshire Supreme Court held that a contract that purported to be signed under seal, but lacked a physical seal, was not a contract under seal under New Hampshire law. More particularly, Douglas held that a scroll (i.e. a written graphic) was not effective as a seal under New Hampshire law. See also, Pequawkett Bridge v. Mathes, 16 7 N.H. 230, 232 (1834) (wax or wafer is required, but a single seal may bind multiple obligors); Carter v. Burley, 9 N.H. 558, 567 (1838) (noting that wax or wafer is required under New Hampshire law, but allowing an embossed Pennsylvania notary’s seal to authenticate a document that was notarized in Pennsylvania pursuant to that state’s law). However, in Allen v. Sullivan R.R., 32 N.H. 446, 449-452 (1855), the New Hampshire Supreme Court liberalized the practice of sealing private documents by allowing an embossed seal to serve the same function as wax or wafer: At common law it was originally held that a seal consisted of an impression upon wax, or wafer, or some other tenacious substance, capable of being impressed. [citations omitted]. * * * Though wax and wafer are most frequently spoken of as the material of seals, yet other things were used. The bulls of the Pope were sealed with lead or gold. [citation omitted]. And in our own State, as well as elsewhere, seals were very commonly impressions made upon pieces of paper annexed by a wafer, gum or paste, to the instrument sealed, or two such pieces of paper 17 were secured to each other, and to tapes passed through the paper, or parchment, of the instrument, by wafer, or other adhesive substance, and the impression made upon one of these pieces of paper. It seems to us, then, that there is nothing necessary to constitute a seal but some material of a suitable character to receive an impression, and an impression bearing the character of a seal upon it. Where wax, or a paper annexed by wafer, were fixed to an instrument in the place of a seal, and with the apparent intention that they should be seals, the court would not look curiously to discover the impression made upon it; but where there was nothing but the impression made upon the paper to indicate that there was a seal, the court would not regard any thing as a seal but such a clear and manifest impression as left no doubt as to its purpose. . . . Most seals have, in this State, not been affixed to wax, or wafer, or to any adhesive substance, but they have been impressed upon paper attached by a wafer or paste, by the effect of which the paper was rendered susceptible of receiving and retaining the impression of the seal. When, then, presses have been contrived of such power as to make an equally distinct and permanent impression directly upon the paper alone, it does not seem consistent to hold that the wafer or paste, whose chief use was to facilitate the making of the impression upon the paper under which it was put, is still requisite, when it has ceased to be either necessary or useful for that purpose. 18 Heretofore, and now, the impression of the seal has been made upon the paper, which seems, therefore, at this day precisely that tenacious substance which is capable of receiving the impression required for a seal. The court are therefore of opinion that . . . an impression of the seal of a railroad corporation, impressed upon the paper of instruments issued by them as bonds, and purporting to be under seal, is a sufficient seal to make the instruments specialties, on which debt may be maintained. As best the court can tell, the New Hampshire Supreme Court has never revisited Allen. In Filip v. Bogdan, 123 N.H. 98, 99 (1983), the court held, without citation or analysis, that a deed that lacked “the customary wafer seal” but contained the words “witness my hand and seal” was not properly sealed.3 Notably, Filip neither overruled Allen’s express holding that an embossed and imprinted seal could take the place of a physically attached wafer, nor expanded Allen to permit 3 At the time the deed was signed, the applicable New Hampshire statute required deeds to be sealed in order to be effective. RSA 477:3 (1977). The Supreme Court held that the unsealed deed was invalid, but that based on the specific facts of the case the purported grantee was entitled to equitable relief. 19 the use of scrolls, graphics or verbiage to take the place of a physical seal. Therefore, this court views Allen as controlling and undisturbed precedent. The parties have not drawn the court’s attention, and the court has not located, any New Hampshire statute that permits what Allen did not. Accordingly, the court determines that the 2013 guaranty agreement is not a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. Therefore, all of plaintiff’s claims are subject to the three-year statute of limitations for personal action set forth in RSA 508:4. Because this case was filed after the three-year limitations period lapsed, the defendants’ motion to dismiss is GRANTED. III. ADDENDUM In ruling on the motion to dismiss the court strived to provide the parties with a workmanlike analysis of the pertinent statutes and caselaw. However, the issues presented do not appear in a vacuum and some historical context is helpful. The 800 year 20 history of enforcement of sealed covenants in common law jurisdictions4 is intertwined in a fascinating way with the 400 year history of statutes of limitations. The present dispute—in which a workaday loan and guaranty agreement is recast as something akin to a sealed grant of property, and is then said to be subject to a limitations period seven times as long as that for ordinary contracts—is the result of historical happenstance, rather than deliberate policy choices. The purpose of this appendix is to explain how we got to this point; but what is written here is not determinative of the court’s ruling. Sealed contracts played an important role in the development of the law but are today anachronistic and 4 See generally 1 Williston on Contracts (4th ed.) §2.2 et. seq. Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Topic 3 introductory note and statutory note; Barbour, The History Of Contract In Early English Equity,pp. 17-40 (Oxford Clarendon Press, 1914), available in PDF at https://repository.law.umich.edu/books/67); Eric Mills Holmes, Stature and Status of A Promise Under Seal As A Legal Formality, 29 Willamette L. Rev. 617, 635 (1993). 21 vestigial. Indeed, in New Hampshire contracts under seal have become virtually extinct. According to both Westlaw and Lexis, the terms “sealed contract” and “contract under seal” have not been uttered by the New Hampshire Supreme Court since 1963 (except when quoting RSA 508:5 in toto in cases not involving sealed contracts).5 Neither phrase appears in any reported or unofficially published decision of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire for an even longer period of time. By virtue of the U.C.C., contracts under seal have vanished from transactions for the sale or lease of goods. 382-A:2A-203. RSA 382-A:2-203; RSA Seals are unnecessary to meet the U.C.C. requirements for notes, drafts, commercial paper, 5 In the 1963 case, Goulet v. Goulet, 105 N.H. 51 (1963), the plaintiff delivered to the defendant a sealed covenant not to sue. Applying Maine law, the New Hampshire Supreme Court held that the sealed covenant was enforceable notwithstanding the lack of consideration. The Court did not comment on any principle of New Hampshire law relating to sealed contracts. Additionally, as noted above, in 1983 in Filip the Supreme Court applied the statutory requirement (long since repealed)that deeds must be sealed to be effective. 22 security agreements and other instruments. Sealed deeds are no longer required to convey real estate. RSA 477:1. While contracts under seal continue to exist as matter of undisturbed New Hampshire common law, it is easier to find a spittoon or ashtray or inkwell in a New Hampshire courtroom than a true sealed contract. Sealed contracts (called covenants and later specialties) were first enforced in the common law courts in the 1200s. At the time, the formality of a hot wax seal imprinted by a signet ring provided an unmistakable, ceremonial, fraud resistant and largely irrebuttable intent to be bound. A sealed and delivered specialty was viewed as similar to a deed, i.e. as a grant of title, rather than as a statement of mutual executory promises. Early writs based on sealed covenants accused the defendant of dispossessing the plaintiff of property, even if the alleged property was an executory promise of future payment. Mutuality of consideration was neither necessary nor sufficient to 23 prevail on a writ of covenant or, later, on a writ of debt or detinue supported by a sealed instrument. By the 1500s, as England was becoming a more commercial and less feudal nation, the common law courts developed the writ of assumpsit. Prior to assumpsit, there was no common law remedy for breach of an unsealed written or oral exchange of promises. With assumpsit, however, proof of mutual consideration was allowed to serve in place of a wax, imprinted seal. Assumpsit also provided a more flexible approach to damages than covenant. Assumpsit and Covenant existed side by side for centuries. However, over time assumpsit won out. Today every One-L is taught the trinity of offer/acceptance/ consideration while the more pedigreed trilogy of signed/sealed/delivered is associated with Stevie Wonder, not commercial law.6 6 Just to be clear, contracts under seal did not need to be signed until the first statute of frauds in 1677. 24 By the mid-twentieth century, many American jurisdictions had eliminated private seals altogether. See Restatement (First) of Contracts, §95, special note (1932) (“In nearly half of the States the distinction between sealed and unsealed writings is abolished.”); Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Topic 3, statutory note (1981) (noting that, “The law regarding contracts under seal has been changed by statute in most of the states.”). In most states where private seals are still recognized, there are statutes or case law that mute the distinction between what was once called covenant and what was once called assumpsit. note. Id., at statutory Some jurisdictions require the plaintiff to prove mutual consideration regardless of the presence of a seal. In other jurisdictions, the seal is only prima facie evidence of consideration. Virtually everywhere, the same measures of damages and the same defenses are made available regardless of whether a contract was sealed. However, it is nonetheless true, 25 as the Second Restatement recognized, that some states, including New Hampshire, have never expressly altered the common law significance of a private seal by either statute or judicial decision. As the legal significance of private seals diminished, many states watered down the physical requirements for a seal. Id. As explained above, in New Hampshire hot wax seals were replaced by adhesive wafers which were replaced by embossed impressions. Elsewhere, physical seals were done away with altogether. In some states simply printing the word “seal” next to the signature line on a mass produced form is deemed sufficient(the theory being that a signor can elect to adopt the seal as his or her own, saving the signor from the hassle of investing in a signet ring or embosser). In other states, the preprinted word “seal” must be must be accompanied by language in the contract itself stating that it is signed under seal. But allowing such terms of art to transmute a contract into a 26 specialty turns the distinction on its head: It was the physical seal that differentiated specialties from mere written expressions of mutual intent. How can a written document bootstrap itself into becoming something that transcends mere writing? Which brings us to the history of statutes of limitations. The common law never provided a fixed limitations period for the filing of writs. Although there were earlier statutes of repose relating to land, measured from the date of various coronations, the first general statute of limitations was the 1623 Limitations Act. That watershed statute provided two, four and six year limitations periods for in personem actions. In particular, the 1623 Act provided a six year limitations period for claims “grounded on any lending or contract without specialty” (i.e. for contracts lacking a seal). There is a direct line of descent between the 1623 Limitations Act and RSA 508:4 (New Hampshire’s general statute of limitations for personal actions). See, 1825 27 N.H. Laws, Ch. 41 (tracking the verbiage of the 1623 statute), later codified as Laws, Title XVI, Ch. 3 (1830) and R.S. 181:3 and 4 (1842). Indeed, virtually every American state, and virtually every other common law jurisdiction in the world, has a statute of limitations for in personem actions that can be traced directly back to the language, syntax and organization of the 1623 English statute. Neither the 1623 Limitations Act nor any other English statute prior to American Independence provided a fixed limitations period for suits on specialties or contracts under seal. Given the formality and ceremony that was needed to create a sealed contract, and given the limited defenses available upon its breach, the exclusion of sealed contracts from the 1623 Act is understandable. Staleness was less of a concern with sealed contracts than with so-called informal contracts. As best this court can tell, the first English statute of limitations for specialties was contained in 28 the Civil Procedure Act of 1833. That statute provided for a twenty year limitations period for suits on contracts under seal. RSA 508:5 (New Hampshire’s statute of limitations for actions on contracts under seal) was first codified in 1842 as R.S. 181:5 and it has not been amended since. Although this judge has not located the particular session law that enacted the statute, it was passed after 1835 and prior to 1842.7 Thus, it was enacted in the wake of the 1833 English Civil Procedure Act and it contains the same limitations period. In New Hampshire, and elsewhere, even as the importance of sealed contracts diminished, the statute of limitations for specialties was left unmolested. It stands today exactly as it was written decades prior to the Civil War when (a) specialties were still very much 7 This judge has electronic access to the session laws through 1835. However, the session laws for 1835 to 1842 are not online and, due to the COVID pandemic, this judge does not have easy access to a library with the paper volumes. The precise date of enactment is not material. 29 in everyday use and (b) the New Hampshire Supreme Court required wax or a wafer to create a specialty. Similarly, whether due to benign neglect or otherwise, there are still specific statutes of limitations for sealed contracts in a large minority of American states. In 1981, when the Second Restatement was published, twenty states had such statutes. Id., at statutory note. The upshot of all of this history—and the point of this addendum—is that “[w]here the seal is still recognized, its principal legal consequence is often the application of a longer statute of limitations.” Id., at introductory note. Indeed, in this case, the only consequence of a seal would be an increase in the limitations period from three to twenty years. This is something that the parties could not accomplish directly, even through the use of crisp and unmistakable language. See, West Gate Village Association v. Dubois, 145 N.H. 293, 298 (2000)(holding that a contractual provision purporting to extend the 30 limitations period for claims not yet in existence is unenforceable because it is against public policy). If the parties cannot extend the limitations period directly, why should they be allowed to do so through the legal fiction of an ersatz seal of a type never previously recognized in New Hampshire? December 7, 2020 ___________________________ Andrew R. Schulman, Presiding Justice 31

					STATE OF NEW HAMPSHIRE SUPERIOR COURT Merrimack, ss MBC Ventures, LLC. Clerk's Notice of Decision Document Sent to Parties on 12/08/2020 v. WIRELESS LINK,INC.; and JAWED SHAIKH 217-2019-CV-00613 FINAL ORDER The matter before the court is defendants’ Revised Motion To Dismiss. Defendants argue that (a) New Hampshire law provides the applicable statute of limitations, (b) that statute is the three-year statute for personal actions, RSA 508:4, and not, as plaintiff maintain, the twenty-year statute for and contracts under seal, RSA 508:5, and (c) this action was filed after the three year limitation period. For the reasons set forth below, the court agrees with defendant that RSA 508:4 is the applicable statute of limitations and that it expired before this action was filed. PREJUDICE. According, the complaint is DISMISSED WITH I. FACTS ALLEGED IN THE COMPLAINT A. The 2013 Line Of Credit Agreement And Personal Guaranty This is a suit for breach of a loan agreement and an associated personal guaranty agreement. In September 2013, defendant Wireless Link, Inc. (“Wireless”) obtained a $100,000 line of credit, good for one year, from Bank of America. Wireless signed a contract captioned “Line of Credit Agreement”(“the 2013 Agreement,” Complaint Ex. A). Wireless’ president, defendant Jawed Shaikh, signed the 2013 Agreement in his personal capacity as a guarantor. Section 8.2 of the 2013 Agreement provides that, except to the extent federal law may apply, the agreement shall be governed and interpreted under North Carolina law. The incorporated guaranty agreement (i.e. Section 9 of the 2013 agreement) contains similar language providing that “this personal guaranty is governed by federal law and the laws of North Carolina.” 2 Shaikh’s personal guaranty agreement also states that “This Personal Guaranty is intended to take effect as an instrument under seal.” It was signed by defendant Shaikh as guarantor with the word “seal” in parenthesis after his name. Shaikh signed a second time, on behalf of Wireless, and once again his signature was followed by the word “seal” in parenthesis. However, the document does not have a wax seal, a wafer seal, an embossed seal, a stick-on seal, or any other indicia of sealing. B. The 2014 Amended And Restated Loan Agreement In October 2014, Wireless and Bank of America entered into an Amended and Restated Loan Agreement (“the 2014 Agreement,” Complaint Ex. B). The 2014 Agreement did not extend the line of credit. Indeed, it expressly stated that “The revolving line of credit feature is closed and will not be re-opened. All amounts outstanding, once repaid, may not be reborrowed.” However, the deadline for repayment of principal and interest was extended by until October 3 13, 2015. In all other respects pertinent to this case, the 2014 Agreement replaced the 2013 Agreement with regard to Wireless’ obligations. See 2104 Agreement, Preface B. The 2014 Agreement left Shaikh’s personal guaranty in place. That guaranty, as originally drafted and signed expressly applies to “any modifications or replacements” of the underlying line of credit agreement). Further, the 2014 Agreement contains a Consent, signed by Shaikh in his individual capacity as guarantor. Section 7.2 of the October 2014 agreement contains a choice of law provision that makes New Hampshire (not North Carolina law) controlling. The 2014 Agreement does not purport to be made under seal. It was signed by Shaikh in his capacity as President of Wireless. after his name. The word “seal” does not appear The Consent, signed by Shaikh in his individual capacity, does not purport to be signed under seal. There is no other indicia of a seal. 4 C. Breach Wireless defaulted on its payment obligations. Bank of America’s rights under the 2013 and 2014 Agreements were assigned several times, most recently to the plaintiff. The plaintiff filed this action on September 13, 2019, more than three years from the date of Wireless’ breach. II. LEGAL ANALYSIS A. New Hampshire Law Provides The Statute Of Limitations For Plaintiff’s Claim Against Wireless Plaintiff’s claim against Wireless must be brought under the 2014 Agreement rather than the 2013 Agreement. That is so because the 2014 Agreement replaced the 2013 Agreement with respect to (a) Wireless’ repayment obligations and (b) dispute resolution. The 2014 Agreement contains a choice of law provision stating that New Hampshire law controls. This court must honor that provision. See Hobin v. Coldwell Banker Residential Affiliates, 144 N.H. 626, 628 (2000) (“Where parties to a contract select the law 5 of a particular jurisdiction to govern their affairs, that choice will be honored if the contract bears any significant relationship to that jurisdiction.”); see also In Re Scott, 160 N.H. 354, 364 (2010); Coldwell Banker Real Estate, LLC v. Brian Moses Realty, Inc., 752 F. Supp.2d 148, 164 (D.N.H. 2010). In this case, the 2014 agreement bore a clear relationship to New Hampshire because Shaikh lived in this state and seemingly operated Wireless in this state. The fact that the earlier 2013 Agreement was governed by North Carolina law is beside the point. B. New Hampshire Law Also Provides The Statute Of Limitations For Plaintiff’s Claim Against Shaikh Wireless’ breach of guaranty claim against Shaikh is brought under the guaranty agreement incorporated within the 2013 Agreement (i.e. Section 9 of the 2013 Agreement). As noted above, the guaranty agreement survived intact even after the 2014 Agreement otherwise replaced the 2013 Agreement. The guaranty agreement 6 included its own choice of law provision that requires the court to apply North Carolina law. However, while North Carolina law applies to the substance of the claim against Shaikh (i.e. to the elements that plaintiff must prove to establish liability, to the measure of damages, and to the elements of defenses and affirmative defenses), this court must apply New Hampshire procedural law. Keeton v. Hustler Magazine, Inc., 131 N.H. 6, 12 (1988); Bartlett v. Commerce Insurance Company, 167 N.H. 521, 526(2015). The New Hampshire Supreme Court generally treats statutes of limitations as procedural for choice of law purposes. See Waterfield v. Meredith Corporation, 161 N.H. 707, 710 (2011) (“[W]e generally treat statutes of limitations as procedural statutes and accordingly apply our own law.”); Gordon v. Gordon, 118 N.H. 356, 360 (1978) (“We have long followed the general rule that a statute of limitations is a matter of procedure and as such the law of the forum applies.”). 7 To be sure, a limitations period can sometimes be an intrinsic, inseparable and vital part of another state’s statutory scheme for the determination of liability. In such cases, the limitations period may be substantive, see Keeton, 131 N.H. at 13-14, but this is not such a case. In this case the plaintiff asserts a generic North Carolina common law claim (i.e. breach of contract) that is subject a generic limitations period. It is also true that New Hampshire courts will engage in a multi-factored choice of law analysis regarding a limitations period in the odd case in which both (a) no party is a New Hampshire resident and (b) the cause of action did not arise in New Hampshire. Keeton, 131 N.H. at 15. However: [I]n any case in which either party is a New Hampshire resident or the cause of action arose in this State, the sum of our above stated forum interests in applying our own statute, in combination with the benefit of simplification afforded by regular application of our own rule, will tip the choice of law balance in favor of the application of our own limitations period to cases tried here. Thus, in such cases, our courts may typically apply the 8 relevant New Hampshire statute without appeal to our choice-influencing considerations. Id. In this case, the defendants are both New Hampshire residents. Therefore, pursuant to the Keeton line of cases, New Hampshire law provides the applicable limitations period for plaintiff’s claims against Shaikh. C. The Applicable Statute Of Limitations Is RSA 508:4 (“personal actions”), Not RSA 508:5 (“specialties”) Wireless and Shaikh claim that the applicable statute of limitations is RSA 508:4. That statute provides a three year limitations period for personal actions, “except as otherwise provided by law.” The breach of contract claims in this case are archetypical personal actions. See State v. Lake Winnipesaukee Resort, LLC, 159 N.H. 42, 48(2009) (noting that while the term “personal action” is not defined by statute it includes common law contract claims). Plaintiff argues that a different limitations period is “otherwise provided by law.” More 9 particularly, plaintiff points to RSA 508:5 which provides a twenty year limitations period for “actions of debt upon judgments, recognizances, and contracts under seal.” Thus, the court must determine whether either the 2014 Agreement (at issue in plaintiff’s claim against Wireless) or the 2013 guaranty agreement (at issue in plaintiff’s claim against Shaikh) is a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. This is an easy question to answer with respect to the 2014 Agreement. The 2014 Agreement does not bear an actual or embossed seal and it contains no language or graphics suggestive of a seal. Therefore, the 2014 Agreement is a plain vanilla contract and the claim for its breach is subject to three year limitations period in RSA 508:4 for personal actions. The analysis of the 2013 guaranty agreement is more complicated. As noted above, although the document does not bear a physical seal, or even an embossed seal, the fine print states that “This Personal Guaranty is intended to take effect as an instrument 10 under seal.” Additionally, the preprinted form includes the word “seal” in parenthesis following the line for Shaikh’s signature. While the relevant New Hampshire case law is sparse, and the controlling precedent dates from another era, it is nonetheless clear that these expedients are insufficient to create a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. The case most on point is Burns Mortgage Company v. Hardy, 94 F.2d 477, 480–81 (1st Cir. 1938). In Burns, the assignee of a note brought suit for its breach. The defendant was the borrower who resided in New Hampshire at the time of the suit. The note was executed in a different state (Florida), where it qualified as a contract under seal. However, the only indicia of a seal was the word “seal” in parenthesis after the borrower’s signature. Both parties in Burns agreed, and the First Circuit held, that the action was governed by the applicable 11 New Hampshire statute of limitations.1 They disagreed, however, about whether that statute was New Hampshire’s (then) six-year statute for “personal actions” or New Hampshire’s twenty-year statute for “contracts under seal.”2 Thus, the question presented in Burns was the same one that confronts the court today. In Burns the First Circuit held that what constitutes a “contract under seal” within the meaning 1 See Burns, 94 F.2d at 480–81: [T]o the extent the validity of a seal affects the obligation of a contract it is to be tested by the lex loci contractus; but to the extent that it affects the remedy for the enforcement of the contract in a forum other than the one in which it was made, including the statute of limitations of such forum, it is to be tested by the law of the forum— the lex fori. 2 In 1938, when Burns was decided, the two statutes of limitations were codified as P.L. 329:3 and 4. P.L. 329:3, which provided the limitations period for personal actions was later recodified without change as RSA 508:4. Subsequent to recodification, the Legislature shorted the limitations period from six to three years. P.L. 329:4 provided the limitations period for suits on contracts under seal. It was later recodified without change as RSA 508:5 and has never been amended. 12 of the New Hampshire statute of limitations is a question of New Hampshire law: It cannot, with reason, be contended that the Legislature of New Hampshire, in enacting section 4 [of P.L. 329, presently codified as RSA 508:5], intended that the words “contracts under seal” should define or embrace any contracts other than those which were regarded by the laws of New Hampshire to be contracts under seal. It surely did not mean to include within those words contracts which might be regarded as under seal by the laws of Florida, statutory or otherwise, or of any other state or country. Burns, Id., at 480. In support of this holding, Burns cited, inter alia, New Hampshire Supreme Court precedent from 1833. In Douglas v. Oldham, 6 N.H. 150, 150 (1833) our Supreme Court held that regardless of where a contract was executed, New Hampshire law will determine whether, for procedural purposes, it was made under seal. Although the New Hampshire Supreme Court has not revisited this issue in close to 200 years, Douglas (and by extension Burns) appears to represent a consensus view among American courts. See, Restatement (Second) Conflict of Laws, §142, comment a (“So if the forum statutes prescribe different periods of 13 limitation for . . . actions on sealed and unsealed instruments, the local law of the forum will be applied to determine whether . . . an instrument is under seal.”); 16 Am. Jur. 2d Conflict of Laws § 95 (“[W]here the question is whether the instrument sued on is a sealed instrument and an action thereon accordingly not barred by limitations, the sufficiency of the seal is to be so tested [by the law of forum]”); Eric Mills Holmes, Stature and Status of A Promise Under Seal As A Legal Formality, 29 Willamette L. Rev. 617, 633 (1993): The law of the forum (and not the law of the state of execution) determines matters of remedy and procedure. If that law regards an instrument bearing the word “seal” in parentheses as not “under seal,” the statute of limitations applicable to unsealed contracts applies. This is true even if the state of execution regards the contract as “under seal” and therefore allows a longer period of limitations. See also President and Directors of Georgetown College v. Madden, 505 F. Supp. 557, 581 (D. Md. 1980) (“[T]he forum's law would be applied to determine, in a limitations context, if the contract was sealed, though the law of the place of contracting would be 14 applied if the question of whether the document was sealed involved a substantive right such as ‘the sufficiency of the instrument as title.’”); Wallbaum v. Martin, 234 A.2d 369 (R.I., 1967)(a promissory note executed in Pennsylvania, that contained the words “witness our hand and seal” and the word “seal” in parenthesis next to the signatures, was not a contract under seal within the meaning of the Rhode Island statute of limitations even though it qualified as such in Pennsylvania); Gaffe v. Williams, 22 S.E.2d 512, 513 (Ga, 1942); Leonor v. Ingenio Porvenir C. por A., 34 N.Y.S.2d 705, 709 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1942); Alropa Corp. v. Kirchwehm, 33 N.E.2d 655, 657 (Ohio, 1941); Coral Gables v. Christopher, 189 A. 147, 149 (Vermont, 1937); Alropa Corp. v. Rossee, 86 F.2d 118, 119 (5th Cir. 1936). Thus, the only remaining question in this case is whether the guaranty agreement is a contract under seal within the meaning of New Hampshire law. It is not. As explained below, New Hampshire requires either a 15 physical or embossed seal and the guaranty agreement contains neither. In Burns, the First Circuit recited the District Court’s determination, which was not appealed by either party, that under New Hampshire law a “contract under seal” must bear a physical wax seal or a physical wafer: [U]nder the law of New Hampshire, the law of the forum, an instrument not bearing a wax seal or wafer is not a specialty or contract under seal. Burns, 94 F.2d at 478. The only pertinent New Hampshire authority cited for this proposition by the First Circuit and the District Court was Douglas v. Oldham. In Douglas (which to refresh the reader’s recollection was decided in 1833), the New Hampshire Supreme Court held that a contract that purported to be signed under seal, but lacked a physical seal, was not a contract under seal under New Hampshire law. More particularly, Douglas held that a scroll (i.e. a written graphic) was not effective as a seal under New Hampshire law. See also, Pequawkett Bridge v. Mathes, 16 7 N.H. 230, 232 (1834) (wax or wafer is required, but a single seal may bind multiple obligors); Carter v. Burley, 9 N.H. 558, 567 (1838) (noting that wax or wafer is required under New Hampshire law, but allowing an embossed Pennsylvania notary’s seal to authenticate a document that was notarized in Pennsylvania pursuant to that state’s law). However, in Allen v. Sullivan R.R., 32 N.H. 446, 449-452 (1855), the New Hampshire Supreme Court liberalized the practice of sealing private documents by allowing an embossed seal to serve the same function as wax or wafer: At common law it was originally held that a seal consisted of an impression upon wax, or wafer, or some other tenacious substance, capable of being impressed. [citations omitted]. * * * Though wax and wafer are most frequently spoken of as the material of seals, yet other things were used. The bulls of the Pope were sealed with lead or gold. [citation omitted]. And in our own State, as well as elsewhere, seals were very commonly impressions made upon pieces of paper annexed by a wafer, gum or paste, to the instrument sealed, or two such pieces of paper 17 were secured to each other, and to tapes passed through the paper, or parchment, of the instrument, by wafer, or other adhesive substance, and the impression made upon one of these pieces of paper. It seems to us, then, that there is nothing necessary to constitute a seal but some material of a suitable character to receive an impression, and an impression bearing the character of a seal upon it. Where wax, or a paper annexed by wafer, were fixed to an instrument in the place of a seal, and with the apparent intention that they should be seals, the court would not look curiously to discover the impression made upon it; but where there was nothing but the impression made upon the paper to indicate that there was a seal, the court would not regard any thing as a seal but such a clear and manifest impression as left no doubt as to its purpose. . . . Most seals have, in this State, not been affixed to wax, or wafer, or to any adhesive substance, but they have been impressed upon paper attached by a wafer or paste, by the effect of which the paper was rendered susceptible of receiving and retaining the impression of the seal. When, then, presses have been contrived of such power as to make an equally distinct and permanent impression directly upon the paper alone, it does not seem consistent to hold that the wafer or paste, whose chief use was to facilitate the making of the impression upon the paper under which it was put, is still requisite, when it has ceased to be either necessary or useful for that purpose. 18 Heretofore, and now, the impression of the seal has been made upon the paper, which seems, therefore, at this day precisely that tenacious substance which is capable of receiving the impression required for a seal. The court are therefore of opinion that . . . an impression of the seal of a railroad corporation, impressed upon the paper of instruments issued by them as bonds, and purporting to be under seal, is a sufficient seal to make the instruments specialties, on which debt may be maintained. As best the court can tell, the New Hampshire Supreme Court has never revisited Allen. In Filip v. Bogdan, 123 N.H. 98, 99 (1983), the court held, without citation or analysis, that a deed that lacked “the customary wafer seal” but contained the words “witness my hand and seal” was not properly sealed.3 Notably, Filip neither overruled Allen’s express holding that an embossed and imprinted seal could take the place of a physically attached wafer, nor expanded Allen to permit 3 At the time the deed was signed, the applicable New Hampshire statute required deeds to be sealed in order to be effective. RSA 477:3 (1977). The Supreme Court held that the unsealed deed was invalid, but that based on the specific facts of the case the purported grantee was entitled to equitable relief. 19 the use of scrolls, graphics or verbiage to take the place of a physical seal. Therefore, this court views Allen as controlling and undisturbed precedent. The parties have not drawn the court’s attention, and the court has not located, any New Hampshire statute that permits what Allen did not. Accordingly, the court determines that the 2013 guaranty agreement is not a “contract under seal” within the meaning of RSA 508:5. Therefore, all of plaintiff’s claims are subject to the three-year statute of limitations for personal action set forth in RSA 508:4. Because this case was filed after the three-year limitations period lapsed, the defendants’ motion to dismiss is GRANTED. III. ADDENDUM In ruling on the motion to dismiss the court strived to provide the parties with a workmanlike analysis of the pertinent statutes and caselaw. However, the issues presented do not appear in a vacuum and some historical context is helpful. The 800 year 20 history of enforcement of sealed covenants in common law jurisdictions4 is intertwined in a fascinating way with the 400 year history of statutes of limitations. The present dispute—in which a workaday loan and guaranty agreement is recast as something akin to a sealed grant of property, and is then said to be subject to a limitations period seven times as long as that for ordinary contracts—is the result of historical happenstance, rather than deliberate policy choices. The purpose of this appendix is to explain how we got to this point; but what is written here is not determinative of the court’s ruling. Sealed contracts played an important role in the development of the law but are today anachronistic and 4 See generally 1 Williston on Contracts (4th ed.) §2.2 et. seq. Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Topic 3 introductory note and statutory note; Barbour, The History Of Contract In Early English Equity,pp. 17-40 (Oxford Clarendon Press, 1914), available in PDF at https://repository.law.umich.edu/books/67); Eric Mills Holmes, Stature and Status of A Promise Under Seal As A Legal Formality, 29 Willamette L. Rev. 617, 635 (1993). 21 vestigial. Indeed, in New Hampshire contracts under seal have become virtually extinct. According to both Westlaw and Lexis, the terms “sealed contract” and “contract under seal” have not been uttered by the New Hampshire Supreme Court since 1963 (except when quoting RSA 508:5 in toto in cases not involving sealed contracts).5 Neither phrase appears in any reported or unofficially published decision of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Hampshire for an even longer period of time. By virtue of the U.C.C., contracts under seal have vanished from transactions for the sale or lease of goods. 382-A:2A-203. RSA 382-A:2-203; RSA Seals are unnecessary to meet the U.C.C. requirements for notes, drafts, commercial paper, 5 In the 1963 case, Goulet v. Goulet, 105 N.H. 51 (1963), the plaintiff delivered to the defendant a sealed covenant not to sue. Applying Maine law, the New Hampshire Supreme Court held that the sealed covenant was enforceable notwithstanding the lack of consideration. The Court did not comment on any principle of New Hampshire law relating to sealed contracts. Additionally, as noted above, in 1983 in Filip the Supreme Court applied the statutory requirement (long since repealed)that deeds must be sealed to be effective. 22 security agreements and other instruments. Sealed deeds are no longer required to convey real estate. RSA 477:1. While contracts under seal continue to exist as matter of undisturbed New Hampshire common law, it is easier to find a spittoon or ashtray or inkwell in a New Hampshire courtroom than a true sealed contract. Sealed contracts (called covenants and later specialties) were first enforced in the common law courts in the 1200s. At the time, the formality of a hot wax seal imprinted by a signet ring provided an unmistakable, ceremonial, fraud resistant and largely irrebuttable intent to be bound. A sealed and delivered specialty was viewed as similar to a deed, i.e. as a grant of title, rather than as a statement of mutual executory promises. Early writs based on sealed covenants accused the defendant of dispossessing the plaintiff of property, even if the alleged property was an executory promise of future payment. Mutuality of consideration was neither necessary nor sufficient to 23 prevail on a writ of covenant or, later, on a writ of debt or detinue supported by a sealed instrument. By the 1500s, as England was becoming a more commercial and less feudal nation, the common law courts developed the writ of assumpsit. Prior to assumpsit, there was no common law remedy for breach of an unsealed written or oral exchange of promises. With assumpsit, however, proof of mutual consideration was allowed to serve in place of a wax, imprinted seal. Assumpsit also provided a more flexible approach to damages than covenant. Assumpsit and Covenant existed side by side for centuries. However, over time assumpsit won out. Today every One-L is taught the trinity of offer/acceptance/ consideration while the more pedigreed trilogy of signed/sealed/delivered is associated with Stevie Wonder, not commercial law.6 6 Just to be clear, contracts under seal did not need to be signed until the first statute of frauds in 1677. 24 By the mid-twentieth century, many American jurisdictions had eliminated private seals altogether. See Restatement (First) of Contracts, §95, special note (1932) (“In nearly half of the States the distinction between sealed and unsealed writings is abolished.”); Restatement (Second) of Contracts, Topic 3, statutory note (1981) (noting that, “The law regarding contracts under seal has been changed by statute in most of the states.”). In most states where private seals are still recognized, there are statutes or case law that mute the distinction between what was once called covenant and what was once called assumpsit. note. Id., at statutory Some jurisdictions require the plaintiff to prove mutual consideration regardless of the presence of a seal. In other jurisdictions, the seal is only prima facie evidence of consideration. Virtually everywhere, the same measures of damages and the same defenses are made available regardless of whether a contract was sealed. However, it is nonetheless true, 25 as the Second Restatement recognized, that some states, including New Hampshire, have never expressly altered the common law significance of a private seal by either statute or judicial decision. As the legal significance of private seals diminished, many states watered down the physical requirements for a seal. Id. As explained above, in New Hampshire hot wax seals were replaced by adhesive wafers which were replaced by embossed impressions. Elsewhere, physical seals were done away with altogether. In some states simply printing the word “seal” next to the signature line on a mass produced form is deemed sufficient(the theory being that a signor can elect to adopt the seal as his or her own, saving the signor from the hassle of investing in a signet ring or embosser). In other states, the preprinted word “seal” must be must be accompanied by language in the contract itself stating that it is signed under seal. But allowing such terms of art to transmute a contract into a 26 specialty turns the distinction on its head: It was the physical seal that differentiated specialties from mere written expressions of mutual intent. How can a written document bootstrap itself into becoming something that transcends mere writing? Which brings us to the history of statutes of limitations. The common law never provided a fixed limitations period for the filing of writs. Although there were earlier statutes of repose relating to land, measured from the date of various coronations, the first general statute of limitations was the 1623 Limitations Act. That watershed statute provided two, four and six year limitations periods for in personem actions. In particular, the 1623 Act provided a six year limitations period for claims “grounded on any lending or contract without specialty” (i.e. for contracts lacking a seal). There is a direct line of descent between the 1623 Limitations Act and RSA 508:4 (New Hampshire’s general statute of limitations for personal actions). See, 1825 27 N.H. Laws, Ch. 41 (tracking the verbiage of the 1623 statute), later codified as Laws, Title XVI, Ch. 3 (1830) and R.S. 181:3 and 4 (1842). Indeed, virtually every American state, and virtually every other common law jurisdiction in the world, has a statute of limitations for in personem actions that can be traced directly back to the language, syntax and organization of the 1623 English statute. Neither the 1623 Limitations Act nor any other English statute prior to American Independence provided a fixed limitations period for suits on specialties or contracts under seal. Given the formality and ceremony that was needed to create a sealed contract, and given the limited defenses available upon its breach, the exclusion of sealed contracts from the 1623 Act is understandable. Staleness was less of a concern with sealed contracts than with so-called informal contracts. As best this court can tell, the first English statute of limitations for specialties was contained in 28 the Civil Procedure Act of 1833. That statute provided for a twenty year limitations period for suits on contracts under seal. RSA 508:5 (New Hampshire’s statute of limitations for actions on contracts under seal) was first codified in 1842 as R.S. 181:5 and it has not been amended since. Although this judge has not located the particular session law that enacted the statute, it was passed after 1835 and prior to 1842.7 Thus, it was enacted in the wake of the 1833 English Civil Procedure Act and it contains the same limitations period. In New Hampshire, and elsewhere, even as the importance of sealed contracts diminished, the statute of limitations for specialties was left unmolested. It stands today exactly as it was written decades prior to the Civil War when (a) specialties were still very much 7 This judge has electronic access to the session laws through 1835. However, the session laws for 1835 to 1842 are not online and, due to the COVID pandemic, this judge does not have easy access to a library with the paper volumes. The precise date of enactment is not material. 29 in everyday use and (b) the New Hampshire Supreme Court required wax or a wafer to create a specialty. Similarly, whether due to benign neglect or otherwise, there are still specific statutes of limitations for sealed contracts in a large minority of American states. In 1981, when the Second Restatement was published, twenty states had such statutes. Id., at statutory note. The upshot of all of this history—and the point of this addendum—is that “[w]here the seal is still recognized, its principal legal consequence is often the application of a longer statute of limitations.” Id., at introductory note. Indeed, in this case, the only consequence of a seal would be an increase in the limitations period from three to twenty years. This is something that the parties could not accomplish directly, even through the use of crisp and unmistakable language. See, West Gate Village Association v. Dubois, 145 N.H. 293, 298 (2000)(holding that a contractual provision purporting to extend the 30 limitations period for claims not yet in existence is unenforceable because it is against public policy). If the parties cannot extend the limitations period directly, why should they be allowed to do so through the legal fiction of an ersatz seal of a type never previously recognized in New Hampshire? December 7, 2020 ___________________________ Andrew R. Schulman, Presiding Justice 31
